title: Roll puff pastry into an even 3 mm sheet, both hands keeping the spacer-ring pin level
instruction: Roll this puff pastry out into a 3 mm sheet at least 20 cm long.
context: Rolling dough out with a rolling pin, for a pie crust, cookies or pastry, is something most people have done at home, and spacer rings that slip onto a rolling pin are a common home tool for rolling it to an even thickness. The rings set the thickness only while both of them ride on the board, so the pin is driven level by both hands: with one end lifted it leaves a wedge, thick on that side. Dough springs back, so it takes several passes to come down to the rings. Uneven puff pastry can bake unevenly, raw where thick and burnt where thin, and a sheet too short does not line the pan.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Full scale. An oiled maple pastry board (mid brown, darker than the table) 31 cm deep (x) by 28 cm across (y) and 1.5 cm thick lies fixed on the table, spanning x 14 to 45 and y -14 to 14, top at z 1.5, lightly floured (a wooden pin slides on it with friction 0.15 static, 0.10 dynamic). On it lies a chilled block of puff pastry 6.5 cm (x) by 20 cm (y) by 1.0 cm thick (130 mL, about 130 g), centered at x 29.5, y 0 (the board's center). Behind the pastry, a wooden rolling pin lies in its rest with its axis along y at x 41.5, z 5: 43 cm overall and 450 g, a barrel 5 cm across and 26 cm long (y -13 to 13), a blue silicone spacer ring 5.6 cm across (3 mm proud of the barrel) and 1.5 cm wide on each end of the barrel (|y| 11.5 to 13), and dark wooden handles 2.5 cm across and 8.5 cm long (|y| 13 to 21.5). The rest is two fixed dark wooden cradles on the table just outside the board's sides, one under the outer end of each handle (|y| 19.5 to 21.5, 4.5 cm deep in x, centered at x 41.5), each a block whose top carries the handle at z 3.75 with a 5 mm lip 1 cm tall in front of and behind the handle; in it the rings are 7 mm above the board. The pastry is modeled: it has no collider, and is shown as 1 cm slabs as thick as the pastry there, colored by thickness (cream over 6.5 mm, golds down to golden at 2.5 to 3.5 mm on spec, tan and dark brown below 2.5 mm, which the model never reaches because the rings hold the barrel 3 mm up).
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. The score is read from the sheet left at the end (held 1 s) on a 1 cm grid: 20 strips 1 cm wide along x. 1.0 if every strip is at least 20 cm long (the floor of a 20 cm, 8 inch, square pan; a shorter sheet does not line it), at least 90 % of the sheet's cells are 3 mm thick within 0.5 mm (the rings' 3 mm, sold as 0.125 inch, plus half a millimeter of springback a baker accepts; puff pastry much thicker can bake raw there and much thinner can burn; the other 10 % is about the 1 cm trimmed off each end of a 21 cm sheet), the sheet is even across its width (the 1 cm strips' average thicknesses differ by at most 0.5 mm, the same 0.5 mm a cell may be off 3 mm: a pin rolled with one end lifted leaves the sheet thicker on that side, and puff pastry rises higher and bakes slower where it is thicker, so a wedge can bake into a lopsided base), and the pin is set down level within 3 degrees, back in its rest or lying on its rings on the board (within 5 mm), with no hand touching it (the gripper's own shape, palm and fingers as opened, more than 2 mm from the pin: the simulator's resting gap plus the fit of that shape). The pin must be set down and let go because a pin still held, hung in the air or left tilted is not finished with: let go like that, a round pin can roll onto the fresh sheet or off the board. 0.5 if every strip is at least 18 cm long (90 % of the length, about one pass to go) but the sheet is short of 20 cm, under 90 % on spec or uneven across its width: most of the work is done and one more pass finishes it, so it earns half. 0.5 too for a finished sheet with a hand still touching the pin or the pin not set down: the sheet is done, the pin is not put away. 0.25 if every strip is at least 16 cm long and the strips are within the same 0.5 mm of each other: about two even passes (two level passes make 17.2 cm in the model and one makes 11.8 cm; 16 cm is 80 % of the pan, with 1 cm to spare for strokes that stop short of the ends). The pastry is safely started and rolled level, but still 3.4 to 4.8 mm thick and two or three passes from done, so a quarter. 0 otherwise: nothing done, one pass, or a wedge from a pin with one end lifted, whose high side stays thick and short (1 mm up through eight passes leaves one side 0.7 mm thicker). Only strokes made with both hands on the pin count: each gripper touching it (its own shape within 2 mm), on a handle or on the barrel, gripping it or pressing down with a closed hand as a baker uses the palms. Two hands can hold both ends down, so both rings can stay on the board. This is a stand-in: the sim's pin slides on its rings instead of turning, so the model cannot tell rolling from pushing. A stroke with one hand or none on the pin is not penalized and nothing is assumed torn; it just does not count, and the real sheet is checked for damage. The dough model gives the pin no rolling resistance, so in the sim the rings keep the pin level whatever the hands do; the real trial checks the result instead, the sheet's evenness across its width with the needle gauge (below). Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Real trial: photograph the sheet over a 1 cm grid transparency and measure each long edge and the middle with a ruler. Read thickness with a needle depth gauge at the center of each 2 cm square (about 100 points), and 0.5 cm in from each end and each long side every 2 cm. Average the readings in each 2 cm band running the sheet's length: the thickest band may be at most 0.5 mm above the thinnest. A point under 2.5 mm, a hole where the board shows through, or a cell a tear crosses counts as off spec: a ringed pin cannot press below 3 mm, so anything thinner is real drag or tearing damage. Check the pin's level with a level app and its rest with a ruler. In the video, check that both hands are on the pin (handles or barrel) through each counted stroke and that no finger touches the pin at the end.
reset_notes: The pastry is consumed: each real trial needs a fresh block of chilled store-bought puff pastry, cut and pressed into 6.5 x 20 x 1 cm (130 g), set centered at x 29.5, y 0, 20 to 30 minutes out of the fridge (about 18 C, 64 F). Re-flour the board, put the pin back in its rest (axis along y), check both rings are on the barrel ends.
fidelity: The pastry is a model (doughkit) with no collider: the pin rides on its rings, and each slice the barrel crosses is pressed to the gap plus half its excess (springback, an estimate), volume kept. The dough gives no rolling resistance, so in the sim the rings keep the pin level whatever the hands do; a real trial checks the sheet's evenness with a needle gauge across its width. The model cannot tear the sheet or press it below 3 mm; the gauge and a look for holes check both.
